extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers studying The Federalist Papers and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: An outline/table-of-contents style listing of the topics, objections, and considerations used in The Federalist Papers to evaluate the proposed U.S. Constitution; each entry records a distinct point or standard used to judge constitutional design and its consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of whether special delegations or class-based representation (manufacturing, learned professions, landholders, merchants, trades) is practicable or desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints include: 'the natural representatives of the mechanic and manufacturing classes' (merchants); 'the learned professions form no distinct class'; 'landholders will be well represented by those in whom they have most confidence, without regard to the extent of their property'; benefits of mixed representation; impracticability of special delegations; men possessing extensive information will best represent all classes; men of strong minds who belong to no particular class can command attention; sympathy among trades is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of internal taxation (Federal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a power of internal taxation in the Federal Congress can be exercised with advantage given lack of local knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations/guidance: members from each State can obtain necessary information; systems of finance are usually framed by a few persons; local disabilities may be ascertained; assessment devolves to discreet persons acquainted with local details; 'the National legislature can make use of the system of each State within that State'; proportion of taxes among the States fixed by numbers; if power proves inconvenient it need not be used and requisitions may be resorted to; question 'why not omit that ambiguous power…and rely on requisitions?' answered (because if convenient it's preferable and its existence gives greater efficacy to requisitions); objections about clashing of State and Federal taxation addressed; minor objections (double revenue officers, duplication by double taxations, odious poll-taxes) considered and answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate militia and call to service
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation to Federal authorities of power to regulate the militia and command services in insurrection/invasion, including uniformity of organization and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points: uniformity in organization desirable and attainable only via Federal authority; objections about lack of posse comitatus provision considered; dangers feared from delegation addressed; approved militia establishment would diminish need for standing military; States retain authority to appoint militia officers as safeguard; objections about ordering militia into distant States considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to principles of republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment whether the proposed Constitution conforms to true republican principles (definition, distinctive characters, historical examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes introductory difficulty of moderate investigation; discussion of predetermined friends/opponents; allowances for Convention difficulties (novelty, combining stability/energy with liberty, partition between General and State governments, interfering pretensions of larger and smaller States); comparisons with Holland, Venice, Poland, England; specific measures such as tenure of offices and prohibition of titles of nobility; argument that proposed Constitution conforms to standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and source of national vs federal government
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proposed government is 'National' or 'Federal' and the real character of the proposed government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points: Government founded on assent/ratification of the People of the several States as such; sources of ordinary powers: House from the People, Senate from the States, Executive immediately from States and eventually by the House; operation and extent of ordinary powers; authority for amendments; whether Convention was authorized to frame a mixed system; commissions and recommendatory acts examined; whether powers exceed Convention authority considered but deemed harmless until approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate quantity and objects of federal power
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination of 'the sum or quantity of power which it vests in the Federal government'—are powers greater than they should be and what are their objects?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects considered include security against foreign danger (declare war, letters of marque, provide armies/fleets, regulate militia, levy/borrow money, levy internal taxes); regulation of intercourse with foreign nations (ambassadors, punish piracies, regulate foreign commerce); maintenance of harmony among States (regulate commerce among States & Indian tribes, coin money, punish counterfeiters, fix weights/measures, naturalization, bankruptcy, post-roads). Each object examined for reasonableness and limits; indefinite character of some authorities discussed and answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Other enumerated powers of Congress and the Union that bear on national efficacy and rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes power to pass laws securing exclusive rights to authors/inventors; exclusive legislation over seat of Federal government; punishment of treason; admit new States; dispose and govern territories and public property; guarantee to every State a republican form of government; protect States against invasion and domestic violence; assume payment of outstanding debts; provide for amendments; establishment of new system when nine States approve; consequences for assenting vs dissenting States considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on State authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions on what individual States may do under the proposed Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit forbiddances listed: establishment of treaties/alliances between States; issue of letters of marque and reprisal; coinage of money; issue of bills of credit; establish legal tender other than gold/silver; passage of bills of attainder; ex post facto laws; laws impairing contracts; establishment of titles of nobility; imposition of duties on exports/imports. Each restriction is cited and its rationale examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and proper / supremacy provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers and provisions that give efficacy to the delegated powers, including necessary and proper clause and supremacy of the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics: power to make all necessary and proper laws for carrying previous powers into execution (necessity in U.S. argued; other methods considered — prohibiting exercise of any power not expressly delegated; positive enumeration; negative enumeration by reserved powers; silence on the subject); remedy for abuse; supremacy of Constitution and constitutional laws and treaties; effect of reserving supremacy of State constitutions considered; oaths for officers to support it; conclusion that no part of delegated powers is unnecessary or improper; whether aggregated powers are dangerous to reserved State authority addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and distribution of federal powers (separation of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proposed Constitution violates the maxim that legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct and how their relations secure republican government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concedes truth of maxim; argues proposed Constitution does not violate it; discusses Montesquieu and British Constitution; examines State constitutions; necessity that departments be connected/blended to give each constitutional control; powers of one department not to be directly administered by another; practical securities examined (insufficiency of naked constitutional restrictions; tendency of legislature to absorb others; examples from history); proposed arrangements to secure mutual checks (little appointment role between departments; independence in emoluments; means/personal motives to resist invasions; division of legislative power; increase of executive veto power).

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Representatives — qualifications and elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for electors' and members' qualifications, term length, apportionment, size, and regulation of elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: qualifications of electors and why not regulated by Congress/State legislatures; advantages of constitutional provision; qualifications of members; biennial term of office debated (frequent elections as security vs need for experience); apportionment by numbers (including treatment of slaves, mixed character of slaves as persons/property); number of House members and difficulty of fixing proper number; objections to small number answered (future population growth, safety and utility); representative's acquaintance with constituents; regulation authority of Congress over elections considered (need for preservation of Union vs danger of abuse; fixing days of election may be important).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment and representation (slaves and persons vs property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and objections about using population (including slaves) as the standard for representation and tax levies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion of whether slaves are property or persons or mixed; Constitution recognizes mixed character; apportionment governed by same rule as levy of direct taxes; replies to objections that slaves do not form basis of local representation; consideration of representing property as well as persons; argument that votes in Congress should be proportioned to comparative wealth of States; measures to prevent falsifying census (same measure for taxation and representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and number of House members
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of how many representatives the House should consist of and implications of small or numerous representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects: importance attached to number; difficulty of determining proper number; small States require smaller ratios; limited delegated powers lessen need for numerous representation; objections (so small a number cannot be safely trusted) considered and answered (population increase, temporary nature); objections about knowledge of constituents and risk of aggrandizement; discussion of quorums and majorities and their effect on lawmaking; prospect of augmenting House as population grows and political checks discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority over federal elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent and limits of Congress's authority to regulate elections for the House of Representatives (and uniform days of election).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductory principle that government must contain means of its own preservation; different depositaries of power to control elections; danger if regulation left solely to State governments; retention of State self-preservation rights; objections about Congress promoting favorite classes considered and answered (improbability, correction by revolt, dissimilarity of Senate and House); provision to require elections in counties where electors reside considered harmless but unnecessary; importance of uniform election days discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate — qualifications, appointment, equality, and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of Senate's structure: qualifications of senators, appointment by State legislatures, equal representation, number/term, and its stabilizing/safeguarding role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: mixed character of Federal government requires mixed representation; equal representation in Senate recognizes State sovereignty and furnishes a security against improper acts; number and term considered necessary institution for republics (security against improper legislation, faction, and for wisdom); history of republics and objections that Senate may become aristocratic addressed; examples from State and national bodies cited; controlling influence of House discussed as counterbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers vested in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific powers assigned to the Senate and their justifications and objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated powers: treaty-making power (importance, best qualified officers, need for secrecy and despatch; objections about supreme authority of treaties and corruption guards answered); appointing public officers; authority as court for trial of impeachments (reasons Senate fit depositary of trust; objections about joining Supreme Court; practicality objections); concerns that these powers may unite legislative and judicial authority; potential for undue accumulation of power and leniency as appointing power considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive department — character and election of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations on the executive: single-person executive, mode of electing President, term, reeligibility, impeachment and removal, veto power, independence from factions/cabals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points: misrepresentations considered; mode of election examined and guarded against tumult, cabal, intrigue, corruption; desirability that sense of People operate and that choice be by competent persons; maintenance of President's independence except on People; President compared with King of Great Britain and State Governors; elected for four years and reeligible; liable to impeachment and civil punishment; power to veto any measure passed by Congress and comparisons to other systems discussed.
